titlePl: Matura PR: Kultura — 180 haseł do gier LingoSpark
titleEn: Matura Extended: Culture — 180 terms for LingoSpark games
blurbPl: Dział Kultura na maturę rozszerzoną: sztuka, media, dziedzictwo i uczestnictwo w kulturze. Fiszki ENG–PL.
blurbEn: Extended-level Culture vocabulary for the Polish Matura: the arts, media, heritage and cultural participation. ENG–PL flashcards.

items.definitionEn: a book that sells in very large numbers
items.example: Her debut novel was a bestseller in twelve countries.

items.definitionEn: a book or film that continues an earlier story
items.example: The sequel is darker than the original novel.

items.definitionEn: a story set before the events of the original
items.example: The prequel explains how the two families first met.

items.definitionEn: a book a person writes about their own life
items.example: In her autobiography she describes leaving Poland at eighteen.

items.definitionEn: a book about another person's life, written by someone else
items.example: We compared a biography of Chopin with his letters.

items.definitionEn: a personal account of a period in the writer's life
items.example: The memoir focuses on her years as a war correspondent.

items.definitionEn: writing that uses humour to criticise people or institutions
items.example: The play is a satire of celebrity culture.

items.definitionEn: a figure of speech that describes something as if it were something else
items.example: The poet uses winter as a metaphor for loneliness.

items.definitionEn: the main character in a story
items.example: The protagonist of the novel is a teenage refugee.

items.definitionEn: the character who opposes the main character
items.example: The antagonist is more interesting than the hero.

items.definitionEn: the voice that tells the story
items.example: The narrator of the novel is an unreliable child.

items.definitionEn: a sudden, surprising change in the story
items.example: The plot twist in the last chapter shocked every reader.

items.definitionEn: an ending that leaves the audience waiting to know what happens
items.example: Each episode ends on a cliffhanger so viewers come back.

items.definitionEn: a collection of poems, stories or extracts by different writers
items.example: The anthology includes three contemporary Polish poets.

items.definitionEn: ordinary written language, not poetry
items.example: She writes clearer prose than most academic critics.

items.definitionEn: a fourteen-line poem with a set rhyme pattern
items.example: Shakespeare's sonnet 18 is still taught in schools.

items.definitionEn: a short story, often with animals, that teaches a moral
items.example: Aesop's fable about the tortoise is known worldwide.

items.definitionEn: a story whose characters and events stand for ideas
items.example: The novel is an allegory of totalitarian power.

items.definitionEn: a contrast between what is said or expected and what is meant or happens
items.example: The irony is that the fire station burned down.

items.definitionEn: a central idea that a work of art explores
items.example: A major theme of the film is loyalty under pressure.

items.definitionEn: the original typed or handwritten version of a text
items.example: The museum displays the author's first manuscript.

items.definitionEn: a company that prepares and sells books
items.example: The publisher delayed the paperback by six months.

items.definitionEn: a person who writes a book that is published under someone else's name
items.example: A ghostwriter drafted most of the celebrity's memoir.

items.definitionEn: an event where an author signs copies for readers
items.example: There was a long queue at the book signing.

items.definitionEn: a person who writes professional judgements of books
items.example: The literary critic accused the novel of being derivative.

items.definitionEn: a novel about a young person growing into adulthood
items.example: The coming-of-age novel is set in a small seaside town.

items.definitionEn: a novel set in the past, mixing invented characters with real events
items.example: Her historical fiction is based on the Warsaw Uprising.

items.definitionEn: stories set in an imagined society that has gone badly wrong
items.example: Dystopian fiction often warns about the misuse of technology.

items.definitionEn: a book so interesting that you want to keep reading
items.example: The thriller is a genuine page-turner from chapter one.

items.definitionEn: a book that authorities have forbidden people to read or sell
items.example: The library held a debate about a banned book from the 1950s.

items.definitionEn: to honour the memory of a person or event
items.example: The mural was painted to commemorate local factory workers.

items.definitionEn: the first public showing of a film, play or work
items.example: The film's Polish premiere is at the Gdynia festival.

items.definitionEn: the place that sells tickets; the money a film takes
items.example: The comedy broke box office records on its opening weekend.

items.definitionEn: a very popular film that makes a huge amount of money
items.example: Summer blockbuster films often rely on special effects.

items.definitionEn: a film that fails to make much money
items.example: The expensive sequel was a box-office flop.

items.definitionEn: films made for artistic value rather than mass entertainment
items.example: She prefers arthouse cinema to superhero franchises.

items.definitionEn: an event where new films are shown and often judged
items.example: The short was selected for a student film festival.

items.definitionEn: the art of camera work and lighting in a film
items.example: The cinematography of the mountain scenes is breathtaking.

items.definitionEn: the written script of a film, including dialogue and action
items.example: He adapted the novel into a screenplay in six weeks.

items.definitionEn: a film based on a book, play or other work
items.example: The film adaptation cuts several minor characters.

items.definitionEn: a new version of an earlier film
items.example: The remake is set in London instead of New York.

items.definitionEn: a film that tells the life story of a real person
items.example: The biopic of the singer has already won two awards.

items.definitionEn: a film or series set in a historical period, with period clothes
items.example: The period drama was filmed in a listed manor house.

items.definitionEn: a shot that shows a face or object in great detail
items.example: The close-up of her hands revealed that she was shaking.

items.definitionEn: speech heard on the soundtrack while someone else is shown
items.example: A calm voice-over explains the archive footage.

items.definitionEn: replacing the original speech in a film with another language
items.example: Polish dubbing of cartoons is often excellent.

items.definitionEn: words on the screen that translate or transcribe the speech
items.example: Watch the original with English subtitles, not a dubbed version.

items.definitionEn: a brief appearance by a well-known person in a film
items.example: The director makes a cameo as a taxi driver.

items.definitionEn: repeatedly given the same kind of acting role
items.example: After the sitcom he was typecast as the clumsy neighbour.

items.definitionEn: a film with a small but very devoted group of fans
items.example: The midnight screenings turned it into a cult film.

items.definitionEn: a film made outside the major studios, often on a low budget
items.example: The independent film was shot in two weeks in Kraków.

items.definitionEn: a performer who does dangerous scenes in place of an actor
items.example: The stunt double jumped from the roof, not the lead actor.

items.definitionEn: an important acting part that is not the lead
items.example: She won an award for a supporting role as the mother.

items.definitionEn: the main acting part in a film or play
items.example: He was offered the leading role after one audition.

items.definitionEn: a full-length film, usually over about ninety minutes
items.example: Her first feature film premiered in Berlin.

items.definitionEn: a film lasting only a few minutes to about forty minutes
items.example: Students submitted a short film of eight minutes.

items.definitionEn: a film or book meant to keep you tense and excited
items.example: The political thriller is set during a state visit.

items.definitionEn: a category of art with shared features, such as comedy or horror
items.example: Science fiction is the genre she writes most often.

items.definitionEn: a person who writes professional reviews of films
items.example: The film critic gave the documentary five stars.

items.definitionEn: an official label showing the minimum age for a film
items.example: The age rating was raised after complaints about violence.

items.definitionEn: a film effect that makes movement appear slower than real life
items.example: The goal is shown again in slow motion.

items.definitionEn: the list of names shown after a film finishes
items.example: Stay for the end credits — there is an extra scene.

items.definitionEn: the people watching a play, film or concert
items.example: The audience rose to its feet after the last aria.

items.definitionEn: a practice session before a public performance
items.example: The cast has a rehearsal every evening this week.

items.definitionEn: the final rehearsal in costume, as if it were the real show
items.example: Nothing went wrong at the dress rehearsal, which made us nervous.

items.definitionEn: an extra song or piece performed after the planned end
items.example: The pianist played Chopin as an encore.

items.definitionEn: when the whole audience stands up and claps
items.example: The premiere received a standing ovation lasting five minutes.

items.definitionEn: an actor who learns a role in case the main actor cannot perform
items.example: The understudy took over when the lead lost her voice.

items.definitionEn: an afternoon performance of a play or film
items.example: We booked the Saturday matinee because evening tickets were sold out.

items.definitionEn: the first public performance of a play or show
items.example: Critics were invited to opening night in the West End.

items.definitionEn: the seats on the ground floor of a theatre
items.example: Our seats in the stalls were close enough to see every gesture.

items.definitionEn: the first raised seating level in a theatre
items.example: A box in the dress circle costs more than a seat in the stalls.

items.definitionEn: a person who shows people to their seats in a theatre or cinema
items.example: The usher asked us to switch off our phones.

items.definitionEn: a short break in the middle of a play or concert
items.example: Ice cream is sold in the foyer during the interval.

items.definitionEn: when the cast return to the stage to receive applause
items.example: The whole company came out for the curtain call.

items.definitionEn: a speech in which a character speaks thoughts aloud, alone on stage
items.example: Hamlet's soliloquy is the most famous speech in English drama.

items.definitionEn: a long speech by one person in a play or performance
items.example: She performed a ten-minute monologue at the drama exam.

items.definitionEn: performing without a prepared script
items.example: The comedy night is based entirely on improvisation.

items.definitionEn: nervousness before or during a public performance
items.example: Even experienced actors admit to stage fright on opening night.

items.definitionEn: a person who writes plays
items.example: The playwright set the new piece in a shipyard.

items.definitionEn: the painted backgrounds and structures on a stage
items.example: The scenery for the forest act was built from recycled wood.

items.definitionEn: objects that actors use on stage or on set
items.example: The props include a vintage typewriter and a suitcase.

items.definitionEn: the area behind the stage, not seen by the audience
items.example: No fans are allowed backstage after the show.

items.definitionEn: a serious play with a sad ending, often about a hero's downfall
items.example: Greek tragedy still influences modern political drama.

items.definitionEn: a comic play based on ridiculous situations and mistakes
items.example: The farce involves four doors and a missing wedding ring.

items.definitionEn: London's main commercial theatre district
items.example: A West End ticket can cost more than a weekend in Paris.

items.definitionEn: small, experimental theatre outside the commercial mainstream
items.example: Fringe theatre in Edinburgh is cheaper and more daring.

items.definitionEn: theatre performed by non-professionals, often locally
items.example: She joined amateur dramatics after leaving the conservatoire.

items.definitionEn: the lowered area in front of the stage where musicians play
items.example: The violinists in the orchestra pit drowned out the dialogue.

items.definitionEn: illegal copying or sharing of films, music or books
items.example: Film piracy costs studios millions, but cheap tickets also help.

items.definitionEn: a long piece of music for a full orchestra, usually in several movements
items.example: The last movement of the symphony is unexpectedly quiet.

items.definitionEn: a piece for a solo instrument with orchestral accompaniment
items.example: The piano concerto demands huge stamina from the soloist.

items.definitionEn: classical music for a small group of players, often one to a part
items.example: Sunday afternoon chamber music in the palace is free.

items.definitionEn: a song for one voice in an opera, with orchestral accompaniment
items.example: The soprano's aria stopped the performance for applause.

items.definitionEn: a musician of outstanding technical skill
items.example: The young virtuoso played the étude without a single slip.

items.definitionEn: a new recording of a song first performed by someone else
items.example: Their cover version of the folk song reached number two.

items.definitionEn: a musician who performs in the street for money
items.example: A busker on the Underground was playing Chopin on a keyboard.

items.definitionEn: played without electronic amplification
items.example: The band did an acoustic set in the bookshop.

items.definitionEn: the main act that a concert or festival is built around
items.example: The headliner came on at half past ten.

items.definitionEn: a band or singer who performs before the main artist
items.example: The support act was better than the famous headliner.

items.definitionEn: an informal word for a concert, especially of popular music
items.example: Their first gig was in a cellar that held forty people.

items.definitionEn: the building or site where a concert is held
items.example: The concert venue has a strict bag check at the door.

items.definitionEn: printed music showing the notes to play or sing
items.example: The choir still prefers sheet music to tablets.

items.definitionEn: a room designed for recording music or sound
items.example: They booked a recording studio for three nights.

items.definitionEn: a company that produces and markets recorded music
items.example: The record label dropped the band after one album.

items.definitionEn: music pressed on a plastic disc, often collected again today
items.example: He bought the album on vinyl for the larger artwork.

items.definitionEn: public or private money given to support the arts
items.example: Cuts to arts funding closed two regional theatres.

items.definitionEn: a group that meets to discuss a book they have all read
items.example: Our book club chose a contemporary Polish novel this month.

items.definitionEn: an informal session in which musicians improvise together
items.example: Saxophonists joined the jam session after midnight.

items.definitionEn: a recording of music performed in front of an audience
items.example: The live album captures the crowd singing every chorus.

items.definitionEn: reaching the highest position on the music charts
items.example: Their chart-topping single was used in a car advert.

items.definitionEn: traditions, skills and practices passed down, not buildings
items.example: The harvest songs are listed as intangible heritage.

items.definitionEn: the right to say, write or create without unfair restriction
items.example: Artists argued that the ban threatened freedom of expression.

items.definitionEn: a picture of arranged objects such as fruit, flowers or crockery
items.example: We painted a still life of apples and a pewter jug.

items.definitionEn: art that does not try to show things as they look in real life
items.example: Many visitors find abstract art harder to 'read' than portraits.

items.definitionEn: a nineteenth-century style that captures light and a moment's impression
items.example: Monet's water lilies are classic impressionism.

items.definitionEn: an early twentieth-century style showing objects from several angles at once
items.example: Picasso's cubism shocked Paris before it became fashionable.

items.definitionEn: art that mixes dream images with unexpected, illogical combinations
items.example: Dalí's melting clocks are a textbook example of surrealism.

items.definitionEn: the European revival of classical art and learning, roughly 14th–16th centuries
items.example: Renaissance portraits often show the sitter with a book or globe.

items.definitionEn: paint that is mixed with water; a picture made with it
items.example: The watercolour of the harbour faded in the sunlight.

items.definitionEn: a painting done on wet plaster, usually on a wall or ceiling
items.example: The church fresco was damaged by damp and later restored.

items.definitionEn: a large painting on a wall, often in a public place
items.example: A new mural on the underpass shows the town's shipyard past.

items.definitionEn: art made by sticking different materials onto a surface
items.example: Her collage combines newspaper headlines with family photos.

items.definitionEn: a three-dimensional artwork designed for a particular space
items.example: The installation art filled the whole hall with hanging fabric.

items.definitionEn: art being made in the present period
items.example: The museum of contemporary art is free on Friday evenings.

items.definitionEn: art in public spaces, including murals and stencils, often unsanctioned
items.example: Street art in the old factory district now draws tour groups.

items.definitionEn: writing or drawings, often sprayed, on walls in public places
items.example: Not all graffiti is vandalism; some pieces are commissioned.

items.definitionEn: mid-twentieth-century art that uses images from advertising and mass culture
items.example: Warhol's soup cans are the most famous works of pop art.

items.definitionEn: a strong cloth surface on which oil paintings are usually made
items.example: The canvas was so large it barely fitted through the door.

items.definitionEn: the board on which an artist mixes colours; the range of colours used
items.example: His palette in this period is almost entirely grey and gold.

items.definitionEn: the way shapes, colours and figures are arranged in a work of art
items.example: The composition leads the eye from the doorway to the window.

items.definitionEn: the technique of drawing objects so they appear to recede in space
items.example: Renaissance painters used linear perspective to create depth.

items.definitionEn: a picture an artist makes of themselves
items.example: Rembrandt painted a self-portrait in almost every decade of his life.

items.definitionEn: a person who buys artworks, often as an investment or passion
items.example: A private art collector lent the sculpture for six months.

items.definitionEn: a fake artwork made to look like the work of a famous artist
items.example: Tests showed the 'Vermeer' was a twentieth-century forgery.

items.definitionEn: repairing and cleaning an artwork or historic object
items.example: The restoration of the altarpiece took four years.

items.definitionEn: a serious newspaper, traditionally printed on large sheets
items.example: She reads a broadsheet on the train, not a celebrity weekly.

items.definitionEn: a popular newspaper with short articles, big headlines and many photos
items.example: The tabloid put a footballer's wedding on the front page.

items.definitionEn: an unfair preference for or against a person, group or idea
items.example: The report was accused of political bias in its headlines.

items.definitionEn: news that is just coming in and is being reported immediately
items.example: Breaking news interrupted the evening film on the public channel.

items.definitionEn: watching or listening to media over the internet as it is sent
items.example: Streaming has replaced DVD rental for most households.

items.definitionEn: a system that allows only paying users to read or watch content
items.example: The investigation sits behind a paywall after the first paragraphs.

items.definitionEn: a person who promotes products or views to a large online following
items.example: The fashion influencer did not say the trip was paid for by a brand.

items.definitionEn: the title of a newspaper article, printed in large letters
items.example: The headline oversimplified a complicated court judgement.

items.definitionEn: an article that gives the newspaper's own opinion
items.example: Yesterday's editorial called for more funding for public theatres.

items.definitionEn: reporting that uncovers hidden facts, often over a long period
items.example: Investigative journalism exposed how the tickets were sold twice.

items.definitionEn: a journalist who reports from a particular place or on a particular topic
items.example: The Warsaw correspondent filed her piece just before midnight.

items.definitionEn: a meeting where someone answers journalists' questions
items.example: The director called a press conference to deny the rumours.

items.definitionEn: a story published or broadcast by only one news organisation
items.example: The paper paid for an exclusive interview with the conductor.

items.definitionEn: false stories presented as news, often to mislead or attract clicks
items.example: Teachers now train pupils to spot fake news before sharing it.

items.definitionEn: false or inaccurate information, whether spread on purpose or not
items.example: Misinformation about the festival times caused huge queues.

items.definitionEn: a sensational headline designed to make people click, often misleading
items.example: The clickbait title promised a scandal the article never proved.

items.definitionEn: presenting stories in an exaggerated way to shock or excite
items.example: Critics accused the channel of sensationalism over a minor protest.

items.definitionEn: the right of newspapers and broadcasters to report without unfair control
items.example: Freedom of the press is weaker where papers need state licences.

items.definitionEn: the evening hours when the largest television audience is watching
items.example: The talent show was moved to prime time on Saturday.

items.definitionEn: the people who regularly read a newspaper or magazine
items.example: The magazine redesigned its cover to attract a younger readership.

items.definitionEn: photographers who aggressively pursue celebrities for pictures
items.example: The paparazzi waited all night outside the hotel.

items.definitionEn: a spoken audio programme you can download or stream in episodes
items.example: I listen to a film podcast on the way to school.

items.definitionPl: rozchodzenie się treści w sieci, viral
items.definitionEn: spreading extremely quickly across the internet
items.example: The dance clip is going viral for the wrong reasons.

items.definitionEn: an online space where you only meet opinions you already agree with
items.example: A social-media echo chamber made the debate more extreme.

items.definitionEn: watching many episodes of a series one after another
items.example: Binge-watching the whole season the night before an exam is unwise.

items.definitionEn: a regular payment that gives access to a service or publication
items.example: A streaming subscription now costs more than a cinema ticket.

items.definitionEn: newspapers, television, radio and large websites that reach huge audiences
items.example: Mass media still shape what counts as a national scandal.

items.definitionEn: radio and television funded to inform, educate and entertain, not only to profit
items.example: Public service broadcasting is expected to cover minority languages.

items.definitionEn: a historic building legally protected from harmful alteration
items.example: You cannot replace the windows of a listed building without permission.

items.definitionEn: the traditional stories, songs, customs and beliefs of a community
items.example: Highland folklore includes tales of spirits in the mountain lakes.

items.definitionEn: art forms traditionally seen as serious and elite, such as opera and classical music
items.example: Some critics still treat comics as inferior to high culture.

items.definitionEn: entertainment and fashions enjoyed by large numbers of ordinary people
items.example: Football and reality television are part of popular culture.

items.definitionEn: the buildings, objects, traditions and knowledge inherited from the past
items.example: Wooden churches are a vital part of the region's cultural heritage.

items.definitionEn: an object made by people in the past, of historical interest
items.example: Each artefact in the case has a label in Polish and English.

items.definitionPl: obiekt z listy światowego dziedzictwa UNESCO
items.definitionEn: a place recognised internationally as having outstanding cultural or natural value
items.example: The salt mine is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a major tourist draw.

items.definitionEn: the sense of belonging to a group that shares language, traditions or history
items.example: Language lessons at Saturday school support children's cultural identity.

items.definitionEn: adopting elements of a minority culture in a way many see as disrespectful or exploitative
items.example: The fashion show was criticised for cultural appropriation of Indigenous patterns.

items.definitionEn: official control that forbids or cuts parts of books, films or news
items.example: Wartime censorship stopped newspapers printing troop movements.

items.definitionEn: the legal right to control how a work is copied, performed or sold
items.example: Copyright in the recording lasts for seventy years after the author's death.

items.definitionEn: legal rights over creations of the mind, such as books, films, designs and inventions
items.example: The museum warned that photographs of the exhibit may still be intellectual property.

items.definitionEn: limited legal use of copyrighted material, for example for criticism or teaching
items.example: Quoting two lines in a review can fall under fair dealing.

items.definitionEn: a person or organisation that gives money to support artists or cultural institutions
items.example: A local factory owner became a patron of the arts after the war.

items.definitionEn: turning art and traditions mainly into products to sell
items.example: Street festivals risk the commercialisation of culture if only brands are visible.

items.definitionEn: presenting information so that it looks better than it is
items.example: The press office put a positive spin on the disappointing results.
